title.en: ExceptionGroup: Report Every Failure, Not Just the First

description.en: A plain `raise` stops at the first problem, so a batch of 100 records tells you about one bad row at a time. Python 3.11's `ExceptionGroup` bundles many errors into one exception, and `except*` handles them by type.

story_variants.en:
## One Raise, One Error... Until 3.11

Imagine checking a file of 100 values. The usual loop raises on the first bad one and stops. You fix it, rerun, and meet the *second* bad one. Ninety-eight reruns later you are annoyed.

The better design is: **keep going, collect every failure, then report them all together.** Until Python 3.11 you had to invent your own container for that. Now the language has one: `ExceptionGroup`.

### Step 1 - Build a group

```python
errors = [ValueError("bad value: 'x'"), ValueError("bad value: 'y'")]
group = ExceptionGroup("parse failed", errors)
print(group.message)          # parse failed
print(len(group.exceptions))  # 2
```

An `ExceptionGroup` takes a **message** and a **non-empty list of exceptions**. It is itself an exception, so you can `raise` it.

### Step 2 - Catch it with `except*`

```python
try:
    raise group
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(type(eg).__name__)   # ExceptionGroup
    print(len(eg.exceptions))  # 2
```

The star matters. `except* ValueError` means: *pull every ValueError out of the group and give them to me as a smaller group.* Notice `eg` is **still a group**, never a single error, even when only one matched.

### Step 3 - A real batch validator

```python
def parse_all(values):
    good, errors = [], []
    for v in values:
        try:
            good.append(int(v))
        except ValueError:
            errors.append(ValueError(f"bad value: {v!r}"))
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup("parse failed", errors)
    return good
```

The loop never stops early. Each failure is parked in `errors`, and one group is raised at the end, so the caller sees all the bad values at once.

### Honest caveats

- The list must be **non-empty** - `ExceptionGroup("x", [])` raises `ValueError`. That is why we only raise when `errors` is truthy.
- Every item must be an `Exception` instance, not a class and not a `BaseException` like `KeyboardInterrupt` (use `BaseExceptionGroup` for those).
- `except` and `except*` cannot be mixed in the same `try`.
- Python 3.11 or newer is required. Older versions have no `ExceptionGroup` at all.

### Key Takeaways

- `ExceptionGroup(message, [errors])` packs many failures into one raisable exception.
- `except* SomeError as eg` extracts all matching errors; `eg` is always a group.
- Collect inside the loop, raise once after it, and only if something went wrong.
- Even a single failure raised through a group stays a group.

`{v!r}` puts quotes around the string, which is exactly what the expected output shows: 'x'.

en: A single ValueError, the first match
An ExceptionGroup holding the matching errors, even if only one matched
It raises ValueError because the list must be non-empty

q.en: Why collect errors in a list and raise once after the loop?

en: The caller learns about every failure in one run instead of one per rerun
Python forbids raising inside a loop

under_the_hood.summary: An ExceptionGroup is an ordinary exception object that stores a message and a tuple of other exceptions; except* asks the group to split itself by type, so one raise can carry many failures.

steps.title: A group is just an exception with a tuple inside
steps.body: `ExceptionGroup("batch failed", [e1, e2])` stores the message in `.message` and the errors, copied into a tuple, in `.exceptions`. Nothing is raised yet; it is an object like any other until you use `raise`.

props.caption: Adding errors one by one to the list before building the group

steps.title: Construction checks its input
steps.body: The constructor refuses an empty list and refuses anything that is not an exception instance. That is why validators write `if errors:` before raising: building the group is the step that fails on an empty list.

steps.title: raise sends the whole bundle upward
steps.body: `raise group` unwinds the stack once. The traceback shows the group and, indented below it, every sub-exception with its own traceback, so no failure is hidden behind another.

steps.title: except* splits the group by type
steps.body: For each `except*` clause, Python asks the group for the sub-exceptions that match the type and passes them to your handler as a smaller ExceptionGroup. That is why `eg` is a group even when one error matched. Whatever no clause matched stays in the group and keeps propagating.

steps.title: The two syntaxes cannot be mixed
steps.body: A `try` uses either `except` or `except*`, never both. Plain `except ValueError` would catch the whole group only if the group itself were a ValueError, which it is not, so it would let the group through.

left.label: except ValueError

right.label: except* ValueError

under_the_hood.takeaway: An ExceptionGroup is a normal exception that holds other exceptions, and except* extracts them by type. Collect failures as you go, raise once at the end, and every error reaches the caller in a single run.
